references.text: The immediate context where God sets the rainbow in the clouds as a sign of the covenant and promises to remember the covenant between himself and all living things, so that the flood will never again destroy all flesh.
Isaiah refers directly to Noah's flood and God's promise that water will never again cover the earth, paralleling the eternal covenant confirmed with the rainbow in Genesis 9:16.

The psalmist praises God's faithfulness and his eternal covenant, where God has established his steadfastness in heaven. This reflects the eternal covenant (בְּרִית עוֹלָם) that God made with Noah and all living things.
God promises to remember his covenant and establish an eternal covenant (בְּרִית עוֹלָם), which mirrors the language used in Genesis 9:16, where God sees the rainbow to remember the eternal covenant.
God heard Israel's cry for help and remembered his covenant—the same theme of God 'remembering' his covenant (לִזְכֹּר בְּרִית) that is central in Genesis 9:16.
Here God's unchangeable promise is mentioned, which can be seen in connection with the eternal covenant God made with Noah and all living creatures, symbolized by the rainbow.
Both verses define God's unshakable 'eternal covenant,' where one establishes its universal foundation and the other elaborates on its familial obligation.
Both verses use a heavenly phenomenon (the bow/the moon) as a 'faithful witness' in the clouds regarding God's unshakable promise.
Psalm 89:29 theologically confirms the promise of an 'eternal covenant,' which is central to Genesis 9:16.
